claim: Animals integrate multiple sources of sensory information across time and space to make optimal and adaptive decisions.
source: In order to make optimal and adaptive decisions, animals integrate multiple sources of sensory information across time and space.
evidence: This is a general statement supported by citations to prior work on sensory integration.

claim: In random-dot motion experiments, performance and neural activity vary proportionally to signal strength consistent with progressive integration of evidence over time.
source: In such experiments, performance and the corresponding neural activity vary proportionally to signal strength in a way that is consistent with the progressive integration of evidence over time (Shadlen et al., 1996; Shadlen and Newsome, 2001).
evidence: Supported by citations to Shadlen et al., 1996 and Shadlen and Newsome, 2001.

claim: Sensory integration is possible by combining information from multiple sensory sources.
source: Besides temporal accumulation, sensory integration is also possible by combining the information from multiple sensory sources (Quigley et al., 2008; Schall et al., 2009; Hollensteiner et al., 2015; Wahn and König, 2015a, 2015b, 2016).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: Multisensory integration often occurs in a statistically optimal way.
source: In the case of multisensory perception, several experiments have shown that integration often occurs in a statistically optimal way.
evidence: Supported by subsequent citations to cue-integration studies.

claim: Humans weight different sources of information according to their respective reliabilities in cue-integration tasks.
source: This has been best demonstrated in cue-integration tasks in which humans perform as if they were weighting the different sources of information according to their respective reliabilities (Ernst and Banks, 2002; Alais and Burr, 2004; Körding and Wolpert, 2004; Tickle et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to multiple cue-integration studies.

claim: Statistical inference has been demonstrated for cortical neurons of the monkey brain with patterns of activity consistent with probabilistic population code implementation.
source: This form of statistical inference has also been demonstrated for cortical neurons of the monkey brain, with patterns of activity at the population level that are consistent with the implementation of a probabilistic population code (Gu et al., 2008; Fetsch et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citations to Gu et al., 2008 and Fetsch et al., 2011.

claim: Perceptual reliability of different inputs is probed through quantitative manipulations of signal-to-noise ratios in sensory integration experiments.
source: In most of these sensory integration experiments, the perceptual reliability of different inputs is probed through quantitative manipulations of the inputs' signal-to-noise ratios (Heekeren et al., 2004; Tassinari et al., 2006; Bankó et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior experimental work.

claim: Some percepts are unreliable because they are inferred only from context and thus intrinsically uncertain.
source: However, some percepts are unreliable not because they are corrupted by noise but because they are inferred only from the context and thus intrinsically uncertain.
evidence: This is a conceptual statement that sets up the study's rationale.

claim: Content is 'filled-in' based on information from the surroundings at the physiological blind spot in monocular vision.
source: This occurs naturally in monocular vision at the physiological blind spot, where content is 'filled-in' based on information from the surroundings.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the blind spot phenomenon.

claim: No veridical percept is possible at the blind spot location.
source: In this case, no veridical percept is possible at the blind spot location.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the blind spot.

claim: The effects of qualitative differences between veridical and inferred percepts that are otherwise apparently identical are unknown.
source: Even though changes in reliability due to noise directly result in behavioral consequences, the effects of the qualitative difference between veridical and inferred percepts, that are otherwise apparently identical, are unknown.
evidence: This identifies a gap in knowledge that motivates the current study.

claim: Differences exist in the processing of veridical and inferred information at the level of EEG responses.
source: We recently reported differences in the processing of veridical and inferred information at the level of EEG responses (Ehinger et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior work by the authors.

claim: A qualitative assessment of differences in reliability exists at the neural level in the form of low- and high-level trans-saccadic predictions of visual content.
source: We demonstrated that a qualitative assessment of differences in reliability exists at the neural level in the form of low- and high-level trans-saccadic predictions of visual content.
evidence: This refers to findings from the authors' prior work.

claim: Active predictions of visual content differed between inferred and veridical visual information presented inside or outside the blind spot.
source: Notably, active predictions of visual content differed between inferred and veridical visual information presented inside or outside the blind spot.
evidence: This refers to findings from the authors' prior work.

claim: No difference was found between low-level error signals for inferred versus veridical information.
source: Although no difference was found between low-level error signals, high-level error signals differed markedly between predictions based on inferred or veridical information.
evidence: This refers to findings from the authors' prior work.

claim: High-level error signals differed markedly between predictions based on inferred or veridical information.
source: Although no difference was found between low-level error signals, high-level error signals differed markedly between predictions based on inferred or veridical information.
evidence: This refers to findings from the authors' prior work.

claim: Inferred content is processed as if it were veridical for the visual system, but knowledge of its reduced precision is preserved for later processing stages.
source: We concluded that the inferred content is processed as if it were veridical for the visual system, but knowledge of its reduced precision is nevertheless preserved for later processing stages.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the authors' prior work.

claim: The present experiment addresses whether assessment of qualitative difference in reliability is available for perceptual decision-making.
source: In the present experiment, we address whether such an assessment of a dichotomous, qualitative difference in reliability is available for perceptual decision-making.
evidence: This states the research question of the current study.

claim: One stimulus was presented partially in the participant's blind spot to elicit filling-in and a second stimulus at the same eccentricity in the nasal field of view outside of the blind spot.
source: Using 3D shutter glasses, we presented one stimulus partially in the participant's blind spot to elicit filling-in and a second stimulus at the same eccentricity in the nasal field of view outside of the blind spot.
evidence: This describes the experimental design.

claim: The subject's task was to indicate which of the two stimuli was continuously striped and did not present a small orthogonal inset.
source: The subject's task was to indicate which of the two stimuli was continuously striped and did not present a small orthogonal inset (see Figure 1a).
evidence: This describes the experimental task, with reference to Figure 1a.

claim: Stimuli within the blind spot are filled-in and thus perceived as continuous, even when they present an inset.
source: Crucially, stimuli within the blind spot are filled-in and thus perceived as continuous, even when they present an inset.
evidence: This is established knowledge about blind spot filling-in that is central to the experimental design.

claim: In diagnostic trials, both stimuli were physically identical and continuous.
source: Crucially, stimuli within the blind spot are filled-in and thus perceived as continuous, even when they present an inset. In the diagnostic trials, both stimuli were physically identical and continuous, and subjects were confronted with an ambiguous decision between veridical and partially inferred stimuli.
evidence: This describes the key experimental condition.

claim: Subjects were confronted with an ambiguous decision between veridical and partially inferred stimuli in diagnostic trials.
source: In the diagnostic trials, both stimuli were physically identical and continuous, and subjects were confronted with an ambiguous decision between veridical and partially inferred stimuli.
evidence: This describes the key experimental condition.

claim: The inset was set to approximately 50% of the average blind spot size.
source: The inset was set to ~50% of the average blind spot size.
evidence: This is a methodological detail from Figure 1a caption.

claim: The global orientation of both stimuli was the same but could be either vertical or horizontal in different trials.
source: The global orientation of both stimuli was the same, but in different trials it could be either vertical (as shown here) or horizontal (not shown).
evidence: This is a methodological detail from Figure 1a caption.

claim: Due to filling-in, an inset stimulus inside the subject's blind spot is perceived as continuous.
source: This example presents an inset stimulus inside the subject's left blind spot. However, due to filling-in, it is perceived as continuous (right column).
evidence: This describes the key perceptual phenomenon shown in Figure 1b.

claim: The task was designed to differentiate between two mutually exclusive predictions: subjects cannot differentiate between the two types of stimuli and answer randomly, or subjects have knowledge about the difference and select the stimulus outside the blind spot in ambiguous trials.
source: The task required subjects to select the continuous stimulus, and it was designed to differentiate between two mutually exclusive predictions: First, subjects cannot differentiate between the two different types of stimuli and thus answer randomly. Alternatively, subjects have implicit or explicit knowledge about the difference between inferred (filled-in) and veridical contents and consequently select the stimulus outside the blind spot in ambiguous trials.
evidence: This describes the experimental hypotheses from Figure 1b caption.

claim: Two stimuli were displayed using shutter glasses with each stimulus presented to one eye only.
source: Two stimuli were displayed using shutter glasses. Each stimulus was presented to one eye only, and it is possible that both are presented to the same eye (as in the example depicted here).
evidence: This describes the experimental setup from Figure 1c caption.

claim: All five experiments included the blind spot location.
source: All five experiments included the blind spot location (green).
evidence: This describes the experimental design from Figure 1d caption.

claim: In the second and fifth experiment, effects at the blind spot were contrasted with a location above it.
source: In the second and fifth experiment, effects at the blind spot were contrasted with a location above it (purple).
evidence: This describes the experimental design from Figure 1d caption.

claim: In the third experiment, the contrasts were in positions located to the left or the right of the blind spot.
source: In the third experiment, the contrasts were in positions located to the left or the right of the blind spot.
evidence: This describes the experimental design from Figure 1d caption.

claim: Both stimuli were always presented at symmetrical positions in a given trial, with position differing only across trials.
source: Note that both stimuli were always presented at symmetrical positions in a given trial, the position of the stimuli differed only across trials.
evidence: This describes the experimental design from Figure 1d caption.

claim: Five experiments were conducted to test the presence of a bias and various control conditions.
source: We conducted five experiments (see Figure 1 and the methods for a detailed description of the tasks). The first one tested the presence of a bias against the blind spot location; the other four experiments were replications of the first experiment with additional control conditions.
evidence: This describes the overall experimental design.

claim: The first experiment tested the presence of a bias against the blind spot location.
source: The first one tested the presence of a bias against the blind spot location; the other four experiments were replications of the first experiment with additional control conditions.
evidence: This describes the purpose of experiment 1.

claim: The first two control experiments tested the existence of biases between the nasal and temporal visual fields at locations other than the blind spot.
source: In the first two controls, we tested the existence of biases between the nasal and temporal visual fields at locations other than the blind spot.
evidence: This describes the purpose of control experiments 2 and 3.

claim: The third control tested whether an opposite bias existed when the task was reversed.
source: In the third control, we tested whether an opposite bias existed when the task was reversed.
evidence: This describes the purpose of control experiment 4.

claim: The last experiment controls whether the observed bias could be explained by probability matching.
source: The last experiment controls whether the observed bias could be explained by probability matching.
evidence: This describes the purpose of control experiment 5.

claim: In experiment 1, 24 subjects performed a 2-AFC task indicating which of two stimuli was continuously striped.
source: In the first experiment, 24 subjects performed a 2-AFC task in which they had to indicate which of two stimuli was continuously striped instead of presenting a small orthogonal central inset (Figure 1a,b).
evidence: This describes the experimental procedure for experiment 1.

claim: The stimuli were presented simultaneously in the periphery at the locations of the blind spots or at equivalent eccentricity on the opposite side.
source: The stimuli were presented simultaneously in the periphery at the locations of the blind spots or at equivalent eccentricity on the opposite side (Figure 1c,d).
evidence: This describes the experimental procedure.

claim: A 3D monitor and shutter glasses were used that allowed for controlled monocular display of the stimuli.
source: We used a 3D monitor and shutter glasses that allowed for the controlled monocular display of the stimuli.
evidence: This describes the experimental equipment.

claim: Each stimulus was visible to a single eye only.
source: That means each stimulus was visible to a single eye only.
evidence: This describes the experimental procedure.

claim: In a given trial, either one or both eyes were stimulated.
source: There were always two stimuli, therefore, in a given trial either one or both eyes were stimulated (Figure 1b).
evidence: This describes the experimental procedure.

claim: Subjects always perceived the two stimuli at the same locations, to the left and right of the fixation cross.
source: Importantly, subjects always perceived the two stimuli at the same locations, to the left and the right of the fixation cross.
evidence: This describes the perceptual experience in the experiment.

claim: There were perceptually ambiguous trials where two continuous stimuli were perceived, and unambiguous trials where one stimulus contained a visible inset.
source: In this experiment there were perceptually ambiguous trials, where two continuous stimuli were perceived, and unambiguous trials where one stimulus contained a visible inset.
evidence: This describes the trial types in the experiment.

claim: In unambiguous trials, an orthogonal inset was present in one of the stimuli and was outside the blind spot and therefore clearly visible.
source: In the unambiguous trials, an orthogonal inset was present in one of the stimuli. Importantly, in these trials, the stimulus with the inset was outside the blind spot and therefore clearly visible.
evidence: This describes the unambiguous trial condition.

claim: Subjects performed with near-perfect accuracy in unambiguous trials, choosing the continuous stimulus in an average of 98.8% of trials.
source: As expected, subjects performed with near-perfect accuracy (Figure 2, unambiguous trials, blue data), choosing the continuous stimulus in an average of 98.8% of trials (95%-quantile over subjects [96.4–100%]).
evidence: This is a data-based finding from experiment 1.

claim: In the first type of ambiguous control trials, both stimuli were presented either outside or inside the blind spot, or one was continuous and the other had an inset both inside the blind spots.
source: In the first type (Figure 2, ambiguous control, red data), one of the following applied: both stimuli were continuous and appeared outside the blind spots in the nasal visual fields (Figure 2, row 3); both were continuous and appeared inside the blind spots (Figure 2, row 4); or one was continuous, the other had an inset, and both appeared inside the blind spots with the inset either in the left or the right blind spot (Figure 2, rows 5 and 6).
evidence: This describes the ambiguous control trial conditions.

claim: When a stimulus with an inset was present in ambiguous control trials, the central part was perfectly centered inside the blind spot and perceived as continuous due to filling-in.
source: In the case when a stimulus with an inset was present, this central part was perfectly centered inside the blind spot (Figure 1a), and in consequence was perceived as continuous due to filling-in.
evidence: This describes the perceptual consequence of the experimental design.

claim: In all four versions of ambiguous control trials, subjects perceived two identical stimuli, and there was no single correct answer.
source: Thus, in all four versions, subjects perceived two identical stimuli, and there was no single correct answer.
evidence: This describes the ambiguous nature of these trials.

claim: In ambiguous control trials, subjects showed a small global leftward bias and chose the left stimulus in 53.6% of trials.
source: In this type of ambiguous trial, subjects showed a small global leftward bias and chose the left stimulus in 53.6% of trials (Figure 2, continuous vertical line).
evidence: This is a data-based finding from experiment 1.

claim: No difference can be seen between the perception of pairs of filled-in stimuli and pairs of veridical continuous stimuli in ambiguous control trials.
source: In addition, no difference can be seen between the perception of pairs of filled-in stimuli and pairs of veridical continuous stimuli (Figure 2, rows 3 vs. 4–6).
evidence: This is a data-based finding from experiment 1.

claim: The ambiguous control trial results confirm that filling-in was accurately controlled in the experiment.
source: This type of ambiguous control trial confirms that filling-in was accurately controlled in our experiment.
evidence: This is an inference from the data.

claim: In the second type of ambiguous trials, one stimulus was presented inside and the other outside the blind spot.
source: In the second type of ambiguous trials one stimulus was presented inside and the other outside the blind spot (Figure 2, ambiguous diagnostic, data in green).
evidence: This describes the diagnostic trial condition.

claim: Selecting the filled-in stimulus is a suboptimal decision because the stimulus presented partially in the blind spot is the only one which could possibly contain the inset.
source: Selecting the filled-in stimulus is a suboptimal decision because the stimulus presented partially in the blind spot is the only one which could possibly contain the inset.
evidence: This is a logical inference about the task structure.

claim: When subjects had to decide which stimulus was less likely to contain an inset, they showed a bias for the one in which the critical information was not sensed directly but inferred from the surrounding spatial context.
source: In other words, when subjects had to decide which of the two stimuli (both perceived as being continuous, and in most cases actually physically identical) was less likely to contain an inset, they showed a bias for the one in which the critical information was not sensed directly but inferred from the surrounding spatial context.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the main finding from experiment 1.

claim: The result of experiment 1 is at odds with both experimental predictions that postulated either no bias or a bias in favor of the veridical stimulus.
source: Remarkably, this result is at odds with both of our experimental predictions that postulated either no bias or a bias in favor of the veridical stimulus.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the main finding from experiment 1.

claim: Experiment 2 was designed to replicate the unexpected result of experiment 1 and evaluate whether the blind spot bias was due to systematic differences between nasal and temporal retinae.
source: The second experiment was designed to replicate the unexpected result of the first experiment and evaluate whether the blind spot bias observed was due to systematic differences between nasal and temporal retinae.
evidence: This describes the purpose of experiment 2.

claim: There is higher photoreceptor density at locations that project to the nasal retina (the temporal visual field where the blind spots are located).
source: There is higher photoreceptor density (Curcio et al., 1990), spatial resolution (Rovamo et al., 1982), luminance discrimination (Pöppel et al., 1973) and orientation discrimination (Paradiso and Carney, 1988) at locations that project to the nasal retina (the temporal visual field where the blind spots are located).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: There is higher spatial resolution at locations that project to the nasal retina.
source: There is higher photoreceptor density (Curcio et al., 1990), spatial resolution (Rovamo et al., 1982), luminance discrimination (Pöppel et al., 1973) and orientation discrimination (Paradiso and Carney, 1988) at locations that project to the nasal retina (the temporal visual field where the blind spots are located).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: There is higher luminance discrimination at locations that project to the nasal retina.
source: There is higher photoreceptor density (Curcio et al., 1990), spatial resolution (Rovamo et al., 1982), luminance discrimination (Pöppel et al., 1973) and orientation discrimination (Paradiso and Carney, 1988) at locations that project to the nasal retina (the temporal visual field where the blind spots are located).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: There is higher orientation discrimination at locations that project to the nasal retina.
source: There is higher photoreceptor density (Curcio et al., 1990), spatial resolution (Rovamo et al., 1982), luminance discrimination (Pöppel et al., 1973) and orientation discrimination (Paradiso and Carney, 1988) at locations that project to the nasal retina (the temporal visual field where the blind spots are located).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Experiment 2 was conducted with a new group of 27 subjects and an additional experimental condition with stimuli displayed at symmetrical locations above the blind spot.
source: Thus, we repeated our experiment with a new group of subjects (n = 27) and an additional experimental condition. In this new condition, the two stimuli were displayed at symmetrical locations above the blind spot (25° above the horizontal meridian; see Figure 1d, purple location).
evidence: This describes the experimental design of experiment 2.

claim: The results of experiment 2 replicate the observations of experiment 1, with subjects showing a bias for selecting the stimulus presented inside the blind spot (12.5%).
source: The results of this second experiment replicate the observations of experiment 1 (Figure 3a): subjects showed a bias for selecting the stimulus presented inside the blind spot (12.5%, CDI957.35–17.49%).
evidence: This is a data-based finding from experiment 2.

claim: In experiment 2, subjects also presented a bias in the control condition, toward the stimuli presented in the temporal visual field above the blind spot (6.63%).
source: However, subjects also presented a bias in the control condition, toward the stimuli presented in the temporal visual field above the blind spot (6.63%, CDI950.77–12.3%).
evidence: This is a data-based finding from experiment 2.

claim: The bias was stronger inside the blind spot than in the control location above the blind spot (paired difference: 6.11%).
source: The bias was nevertheless stronger inside the blind spot (paired difference: 6.11%, CDI951.16–10.78%).
evidence: This is a data-based finding from experiment 2.

claim: In addition to the bias inside the blind spot area, subjects showed a smaller bias for stimuli presented to the nasal retina (temporal visual field).
source: In summary, additionally to the bias inside of the blind spot area, we observed that subjects also showed a smaller bias for stimuli presented to the nasal retina (temporal visual field).
evidence: This is a summary of findings from experiment 2.

claim: Experiment 3 was performed on a new group of 24 subjects to better delineate the distribution of bias across the temporal visual field and clarify if the blind spot location is special.
source: To better delineate the distribution of bias across the temporal visual field and to clarify if the blind spot location is, in fact, special, we performed a third experiment on a new group of subjects (n = 24).
evidence: This describes the purpose and design of experiment 3.

claim: In experiment 3, biases in the blind spot were compared to two other control conditions flanking the blind spot region from either the left or the right.
source: Here, we compared biases in the blind spot to two other control conditions flanking the blind spot region from either the left or the right (Figure 3b).
evidence: This describes the experimental design of experiment 3.

claim: In experiments 1, 2, and 3, a bias was observed that is specific to the blind spot region.
source: In this experiment, as in experiments 1 and 2, we observed a bias that is specific to the blind spot region.
evidence: This is a summary of findings from experiments 1-3.

claim: Experiment 4 was performed with a new group of 25 subjects and was identical to experiment 1 except that subjects' task was to choose the stimulus with an inset instead of the continuous one.
source: To confirm this, we performed a fourth experiment with a new group of subjects (n = 25). This experiment was identical to the first experiment, except that in this case, the subjects' task was to choose the stimulus with an inset, instead of the continuous one.
evidence: This describes the experimental design of experiment 4.

claim: In experiment 4, if a filled-in stimulus is considered a more reliable exemplar of a continuous stimulus, the non blind spot stimulus should be preferred in the diagnostic trials.
source: In this case, if a filled-in stimulus is indeed considered a more reliable exemplar of a continuous stimulus, the non blind spot stimulus should be preferred in the diagnostic trials.
evidence: This is a prediction for experiment 4.

claim: In experiment 4, subjects showed a bias for selecting the stimulus presented outside the blind spot (7.74%).
source: This was the case; subjects showed a bias for selecting the stimulus presented outside the blind spot (7.74%, CDI951.56–13.68%, Figure 4a), thus resulting in the expected reversal of the bias pattern observed in the first three experiments.
evidence: This is a data-based finding from experiment 4.

claim: The result of experiment 4 resulted in the expected reversal of the bias pattern observed in the first three experiments.
source: This was the case; subjects showed a bias for selecting the stimulus presented outside the blind spot (7.74%, CDI951.56–13.68%, Figure 4a), thus resulting in the expected reversal of the bias pattern observed in the first three experiments.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the finding from experiment 4.

claim: The bias pattern in experiment 4 is suboptimal because the filled-in stimulus is the one that could conceal the target.
source: This pattern is again suboptimal, since this time the filled-in stimulus is the one that could conceal the target.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the finding from experiment 4.

claim: The result of experiment 4 indicates that the observed biases do not correspond to an unspecific response bias for the blind spot, and instead are a consequence of considering the inferred percepts as more reliable exemplars of a continuous stimulus.
source: The result of this experiment indicates that the observed biases do not correspond to an unspecific response bias for the blind spot, and instead are a consequence of considering the inferred percepts as more reliable exemplars of a continuous stimulus.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the finding from experiment 4.

claim: Experiment 5 was performed to evaluate whether the observed bias for a filled-in stimulus was a result of subjects using a probability matching heuristic.
source: We performed a final control to evaluate whether the observed bias for a filled-in stimulus was not a result of subjects using a probability matching heuristic.
evidence: This describes the purpose of experiment 5.

claim: It is impossible to experience an inset in the blind spot, so the base rate of continuous stimuli at that location is 1.0.
source: As it is impossible to experience an inset in the blind spot, the base rate of continuous stimuli at that location is 1.0.
evidence: This is a logical inference about the task structure.

claim: If subjects use probability matching, they should show a bias for the location where they experienced exclusively continuous stimuli during unambiguous trials.
source: Therefore, when confronted with two stimuli that are apparently identical, one inside and one outside the blind spot, subjects might just apply the base rate they have learned instead of relying on a perceptual estimate. If this is the case, subjects should show a bias for the location where they experienced exclusively continuous stimuli during unambiguous trials, which could result in a bias pattern similar to the one observed in experiments 1–3.
evidence: This is a prediction for experiment 5 under the probability matching hypothesis.

claim: Experiment 5 was similar to experiment 2, with control trials presenting stimuli above the blind spot, but subjects never experienced an inset in the temporal field in the above positions during unambiguous trials.
source: To evaluate this alternative explanation, we performed a further experiment with the same group of subjects that participated in experiment 4. Experiment 5 was similar to experiment 2, with control trials presenting stimuli above the blind spot. However, in contrast to experiment 2, subjects never experienced an inset in the temporal field in the above positions during unambiguous trials (see Figure 1—figure supplement 1 for a detailed overview of trial randomization).
evidence: This describes the experimental design of experiment 5.

claim: In experiment 5, the base rate of occurrence of a continuous stimulus in the temporal field was identical for both the above and blind spot locations.
source: This results in an identical base rate of occurrence of a continuous stimulus in the temporal field for both the above and blind spot locations.
evidence: This is a logical consequence of the experimental design of experiment 5.

claim: If the behavior observed in previous experiments was a result of probability matching, in experiment 5 the same bias should be observed at both the blind spot and the temporal field above locations.
source: Consequently, if the behavior observed in the previous experiments was a result of probability matching, in this experiment we should observe the same bias at both the blind spot and the temporal field above locations.
evidence: This is a prediction for experiment 5 under the probability matching hypothesis.

claim: The same group of subjects participated in experiments 4 and 5, allowing for within-subjects comparison between the two tasks.
source: The same group of subjects participated in experiment 4 and 5, allowing us to make a within subjects comparison between the two tasks.
evidence: This describes the experimental design.

claim: Subjects' performance in experiments 4 and 5 was negatively correlated (r = −0.61, p=0.002).
source: Subjects' performance in these two tasks was negatively correlated (r = −0.61, p=0.002, see Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a data-based finding from experiments 4 and 5.

claim: Taking the task reversal of experiment 4 into account, the negative correlation indicates that subjects were consistently biased to consider the inferred filled-in stimulus a better exemplar of a continuous stimulus.
source: Taking the task reversal of experiment 4 into account, this result indicates that subjects were consistently biased to consider the inferred filled-in stimulus a better exemplar of a continuous stimulus.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the correlation finding.

claim: The result of experiment 5 gives evidence that the bias for the filled-in stimulus was not a consequence of subjects matching the base rate of the occurrence of different stimuli during unambiguous trials.
source: The result of experiment 5 thus gives evidence that the bias for the filled-in stimulus was not a consequence of subjects matching the base rate of the occurrence of different stimuli during unambiguous trials.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the findings from experiment 5.

claim: A bias for the temporal visual field, especially the blind spot, could be reflected in the distribution of reaction times.
source: A bias for the temporal visual field, especially the blind spot, could also be reflected in the distribution of reaction times.
evidence: This introduces the reaction time analysis.

claim: The reaction time analysis was not a planned comparison and is explorative.
source: The reaction time analysis was not a planned comparisons, thus, in contrast to the other analyses presented here, it is explorative.
evidence: This clarifies the nature of the reaction time analysis.

claim: In experiment 1, an average reaction time of 637 ms was observed.
source: In the first experiment, we observed an average reaction time of 637 ms (minimum subject average: 394 ms, maximum 964 ms; Figure 5).
evidence: This is a data-based finding from experiment 1.

claim: In experiment 1, after excluding three outliers, reaction times were 13 ms faster when selecting the blind spot region.
source: In the first experiment, after excluding three outliers, we observed this effect with a median posterior effect size of 13 ms faster reaction times when selecting the blind spot region (CDI95%  2–42 ms).
evidence: This is a data-based finding from experiment 1.

claim: Three outliers were identified visually and removed because they were distinctively different from the rest of the population, with a mean 5.2 SD away from the remaining subjects.
source: The three outliers (on the right of the vertical dashed line in Figure 5) were identified visually and removed because they were distinctively different from the rest of the population. The mean of the outliers was 5.2 SD away from the remaining subjects.
evidence: This describes the data processing for the reaction time analysis.

claim: The outliers were in the same direction of the reaction time effect and did not change its significance.
source: The outliers were nevertheless in the same direction of the reaction time effect and did not change its significance (with outliers, 63 ms, CDI957–124 ms).
evidence: This describes the robustness of the reaction time finding.

claim: Faster reaction times while selecting the blind spot stimulus were not present individually in experiments 2, 3, 4, and 5.
source: However, faster reaction times while selecting the blind spot stimulus were not present individually in the other four experiments. The nominal differences were in the same direction as experiment 1 but not significant (Exp.2: 4 ms, CDI95−14–23 ms; Exp.3: 22 ms. CDI95 −3–39 ms; Exp.4: −1 ms CDI95 −20–21 ms; Exp.5: 4 ms CDI95 −15–23 ms).
evidence: This is a data-based finding from experiments 2-5.

claim: Non-significant reaction time results were obtained for the other locations tested (above, outward, inward).
source: Non-significant results were obtained for the other locations tested (above Exp.2: 8 ms, CDI95 −38–53 ms; above Exp.4: 8 ms CDI95 −17–32 ms; outward: 2 ms CDI95 −13–16 ms; inward: 4 ms, CDI95 −29–37 ms).
evidence: This is a data-based finding from the control locations.

claim: After combining all data (without experiment 4), a reduced reaction time for decisions for the blind spot stimulus of 10 ms was observed.
source: After combining all data (without experiment 4 as the task was reversed), we observed a reduced reaction time for decisions for the blind spot stimulus with 10 ms (CDI952–17 ms) but not in any other location.
evidence: This is a data-based finding from the combined analysis.

claim: The small reaction time bias is not found in any experiment individually (except Exp. 1) but only after pooling over experiments and should be interpreted cautiously.
source: We do not find this small bias in any experiment individually (except Exp. 1) but only after pooling over experiments and therefore, we should interpret it cautiously.
evidence: This is a cautious interpretation of the reaction time findings.

claim: Subjects selected stimuli in the blind spot slightly faster than stimuli outside the blind spot, but the same effect does not appear for the other temporal control locations.
source: In conclusion, subjects selected stimuli in the blind spot slightly faster than stimuli outside the blind spot. The same effect does not appear for the other temporal control locations.
evidence: This is a summary of the reaction time findings.

claim: No differences were found between the temporal field effects at locations other than the blind spots (inward, outward, and above).
source: In the combined model, we did not find any differences between the temporal field effects at locations other than the blind spots (Figure 6, fourth last to second last row). That is, the temporal field effects of the locations inward, outward and above were not different from each other.
evidence: This is a data-based finding from the combined model.

claim: When presenting one stimulus in the blind spot against the equidistant nasal location, subjects are 13.82% more likely to choose the stimulus in the blind spot.
source: Keeping everything else constant, we observed that if we present one stimulus in the blind spot against the equidistant nasal location, subjects are 13.82% (CDI9510.84–16.78%, t-test, t = 8.7, df = 98, p<0.001) more likely to choose the stimulus in the blind spot.
evidence: This is a data-based finding from the combined model.

claim: The blind spot bias is stronger than the effect observed elsewhere in the temporal field by 9.35%.
source: This bias is stronger than the effect observed elsewhere in the temporal field by 9.35% (CDI95  6.25%–12.47%; paired t-test, t = 4.8, df = 74, p<0.001).
evidence: This is a data-based finding from the combined model.

claim: Subjects showed a robust bias for the blind spot locations that could not be explained by a non-specific bias for the temporal visual field.
source: In summary, subjects showed a robust bias for the blind spot locations that could not be explained by a non-specific bias for the temporal visual field.
evidence: This is a summary of the combined findings.

claim: When confronted with an ambiguous choice between veridical and inferred sensory information, human subjects showed a suboptimal bias for inferred information.
source: In conclusion, when confronted with an ambiguous choice between veridical and inferred sensory information, human subjects showed a suboptimal bias for inferred information.
evidence: This is the main conclusion of the study.

claim: When confronted with identical physical stimulation, subjects showed a consistent bias for blind spot inferred percepts which was stronger than the bias at any other location in the temporal visual field.
source: When confronted with identical physical stimulation, subjects showed a consistent bias for blind spot inferred percepts which was stronger than the bias at any other location in the temporal visual field.
evidence: This is a summary statement of the main finding.

claim: Subjects must possess at least implicit information about whether a percept originates from the blind spot in order to show a bias for or against it.
source: Our interpretation takes the results at face value: subjects must possess at least implicit information about whether a percept originates from the blind spot in order to show a bias for or against it.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the findings.

claim: Perceptual decision-making can rely more on inferred than veridical information, even when there is some knowledge about the reduced reliability of the inferred input available in the brain.
source: At the same time, the veridical information from the other stimulus is also available. This indicates that perceptual decision-making can rely more on inferred than veridical information, even when there is some knowledge about the reduced reliability of the inferred input available in the brain (Ehinger et al., 2015).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the findings, supported by citation to prior work.

claim: The reaction time analyses indicated a faster evidence accumulation for the inferred percepts.
source: This is also supported by the results of the reaction time analyses that indicated a faster evidence accumulation for the inferred percepts.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the reaction time findings.

claim: The implicit knowledge that a filled-in stimulus is objectively less reliable does not seem to be used for perceptual decision-making.
source: In other words, the implicit knowledge that a filled-in stimulus is objectively less reliable does not seem to be used for perceptual decision-making.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the findings.

claim: This suboptimal decision between qualitatively different veridical and inferred inputs is in contrast to properties of standard sensory integration where reduced reliability from noisy but veridical signals results in corresponding weighting of inputs and optimal decisions.
source: This suboptimal decision between qualitatively different veridical and inferred inputs is in contrast to properties of standard sensory integration. There, reduced reliability derived from noisy but veridical signals results in a corresponding weighting of inputs and consequently in optimal decisions (Körding et al., 2007).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the findings in the context of prior research.

claim: The filled-in percept is based on information sensed by the region around the blind spot in the nasal retina.
source: First, although the filled-in percept is by definition independent of the stimulus within the blind spot, it is nevertheless based on the information sensed by the region around the blind spot in the nasal retina.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation of the findings.

claim: An area in the nasal retina around the blind spot region that has a lower contrast threshold might show stronger neuronal signals for super-threshold stimuli.
source: We might assume that an area, e.g. in the nasal retina around the blind spot region, that has a lower contrast threshold also shows stronger neuronal signals for super-threshold stimuli.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation of the findings.

claim: Differences in physiological properties of nasal and temporal retinae might be transferred to the filling-in process making it the 'better' candidate stimulus in an ambiguous condition.
source: This could in principle lead to a filled-in stimulus with increased salience as compared to the veridical stimulus. Effectively, this explanation proposes that differences in physiological properties of nasal and temporal retinae are transferred to the filling-in process making it the 'better' candidate stimulus in an ambiguous condition.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation of the findings.

claim: There is evidence for the superiority of the blind spot in a Vernier task, with areas around the blind spot showing greater performance compared to areas at similar eccentric locations in the nasal visual field.
source: There is also some evidence for the superiority of the blind spot in a Vernier task (Crossland and Bex, 2009). The areas around the blind spot showed greater performance compared to areas at similar eccentric locations in the nasal visual field.
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: It is unclear whether the superiority of the blind spot in a Vernier task goes beyond the temporal/nasal bias.
source: It is still unclear whether this goes over and beyond the aforementioned temporal/nasal bias.
evidence: This is a statement about uncertainty in the literature.

claim: The sensitivity in the region corresponding to the blind spot in the other eye is enhanced compared to regions at similar eccentricities.
source: Unfortunately, this explanation runs into the problem that the sensitivity in the region corresponding to the blind spot in the other eye is also enhanced compared to regions at similar eccentricities (Wolf and Morandi, 1962; Midgley, 1998).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Differences between the eyes in the area around the blind spot should be the smallest within the contrast between temporal and nasal retina.
source: This suggests that differences between the eyes in the area around the blind spot should be the smallest within the contrast between temporal and nasal retina.
evidence: This is an inference from prior research findings.

claim: Temporal-nasal differences were explicitly controlled for in experiments 2 and 3, and it was found that this is not enough to explain the effect specific to the blind spot.
source: Moreover, we explicitly controlled for temporal-nasal differences in experiments 2 and 3, and found that it is not enough to explain the effect specific to the blind spot.
evidence: This is a summary of the experimental findings.

claim: An explanation of the observed effects based on known differences in retinal properties is currently tentative at best.
source: Thus, an explanation of the observed effects based on known differences in retinal properties is currently tentative at best.
evidence: This is a conclusion about the limitations of one explanation.

claim: An alternative explanation is based on the framework of predictive coding.
source: An alternative explanation is based on the framework of predictive coding (Friston et al., 2006, 2012; Summerfield and de Lange, 2014).
evidence: This introduces an alternative explanation with citations.

claim: Context information of static stimuli would be used to predict local stimulus properties leading to the phenomenon of filling-in.
source: Specifically, context information of static stimuli would be used to predict local stimulus properties leading to the phenomenon of filling-in.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation based on predictive coding.

claim: The predicted sensory input would be compared to the incoming sensory input, and an error signal representing the mismatch would be returned.
source: The predicted sensory input would then be compared to the incoming sensory input, and an error signal representing the mismatch would be returned.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation based on predictive coding.

claim: In the absence of veridical information, no deviation and thus no error signal would occur.
source: In the absence of veridical information, no deviation and thus no error signal would occur.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation based on predictive coding.

claim: The filled-in signal might have less noise, resulting in a smaller prediction error and higher credibility at later stages.
source: Effectively, the filled-in signal might have less noise. Reduced noise, in turn, results in a smaller prediction error and higher credibility at later stages.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation based on predictive coding.

claim: A faster reaction time to the filled-in stimulus compared to the veridical stimulus could suggest that the integration process is biased with less noise.
source: A faster reaction time to the filled-in stimulus compared to the veridical stimulus could suggest that the integration process is indeed biased with less noise.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the reaction time findings.

claim: The results reported seem compatible with the predictive coding framework, but this explanation presently remains vague and speculative.
source: In summary, although the results reported here seem compatible with the predictive coding framework, this explanation presently remains vague and speculative.
evidence: This is a cautious statement about the speculative nature of the predictive coding explanation.

claim: A new behavioral effect was found where subjects prefer a partially inferred stimulus to a veridical one.
source: In conclusion, we find a new behavioral effect where subjects prefer a partially inferred stimulus to a veridical one.
evidence: This is the main conclusion of the study.

claim: Though both stimuli appear to be continuous, the filled-in one could hide an inset and is therefore less reliable.
source: Though both appear to be continuous, the filled-in one could hide an inset and is, therefore, less reliable.
evidence: This is a logical statement about the task structure.

claim: In this perceptual decision-making task, subjects do not make use of high-level assessments about the reliability of the filled-in stimulus.
source: In this perceptual decision-making task, subjects do not make use of high-level assessments about the reliability of the filled-in stimulus.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the findings.

claim: Subjects prefer the unreliable percept.
source: Even more so, they prefer the unreliable percept.
evidence: This is a summary statement of the main finding.

source: Overall, 175 subjects took part in the experiments.

source: After a fixation period of 500 ms, we presented two stimuli simultaneously to the left and right of the fixation cross.

source: Subjects were instructed to indicate via button press (left or right) which stimulus was continuous.

source: Each stimulus was presented either in the temporal or nasal field of view.

claim: There are four within-subject factors, resulting in eight parameters: two main factors representing whether the left and right stimulus was inside or outside the temporal field, location factor with up to three levels, interactions between location and temporal presentation, and answer(t-1).
source: In total, we have four within-subject factors, resulting in eight parameters: There are two main factors representing whether the left, and respectively the right, stimulus was inside or outside the temporal field. Depending on the experiment, the main factor location had up to three levels: the stimuli were presented outward (Exp. 3), inward (Exp. 3), above (Exp 2, 5) or on (all experiments) the blind spot. In addition, we modeled the interactions between location and whether the left stimulus (and the right stimulus, respectively) was shown temporally. In order to assure independence of observation, an additional within-subject main factor answer(t-1) was introduced, which models the current answer based on the previous one.
evidence: This is a methodological detail about the statistical model.

claim: All within-subject effects were modeled using random slopes clustered by subject and a random intercept for the subjects.
source: In frequentist linear modeling terms, all within-subject effects were modeled using random slopes clustered by subject and a random intercept for the subjects.
evidence: This is a methodological detail about the statistical model.

claim: Treatment coding was used for all factors.
source: We used treatment coding for all factors and interpreted the coefficients accordingly.
evidence: This is a methodological detail about the statistical model.

claim: Implicit, improper, uniform priors from negative to positive infinity were placed on the mean and 0 to infinity for the standard deviations of parameters.
source: We did not make use of prior information in the analysis of our data. We placed implicit, improper, uniform priors from negative to positive infinity on the mean and 0 to infinity for the standard deviations of our parameters, the default priors of STAN.
evidence: This is a methodological detail about the Bayesian analysis.

claim: Six mcmc-chains using 2000 iterations each were used, with 50% used for the warm-up period.
source: We used six mcmc-chains using 2000 iterations each, with 50% used for the warm-up period.
evidence: This is a methodological detail about the Bayesian analysis.

claim: Convergence was visually confirmed through autocorrelation functions and trace plots, and scale reduction factors indicated convergence (Rhat < 1.1).
source: We visually confirmed convergence through autocorrelation functions and trace plots, then calculated the scale reduction factors (Gelman et al., 2014), which indicated convergence (Rhat < 1.1).
evidence: This is a methodological detail about model validation, supported by citation.

claim: Posterior predictive checks were evaluated to test for model adequacy.
source: Posterior predictive model checks were evaluated to test for model adequacy (Gelman et al., 2013).
evidence: This is a methodological detail about model validation, supported by citation.

claim: Posterior predictive checks work on the rationale that newly generated data based on the model fit should be indistinguishable from the data that the model was fitted by originally.
source: Posterior predictive checks work on the rationale that newly generated data based on the model fit should be indistinguishable from the data that the model was fitted by originally.
evidence: This is a methodological explanation about posterior predictive checks.

claim: Posterior predictive checks were performed on two levels: trial and subject.
source: Due to our hierarchical mixed model, we perform posterior predictive checks on two levels: trial, and subject.
evidence: This is a methodological detail about model validation.

claim: The posterior predictive model checks show that the model adequately captures the diverse behavior of subjects and correctly models the blind spot effect on a population basis.
source: Taken together, these posterior predictive model checks show that we adequately capture the very diverse behavior of our subjects but also correctly model the blind spot effect on a population basis.
evidence: This is a conclusion about model validation based on the checks shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2.

claim: Subjects with a dominant right eye showed a preference to the right stimulus over the left one, irrespective of whether the stimulus was visible through the left or right eye.
source: Thus subjects with a dominant right eye also showed a preference to the right stimulus over the left one, irrespective of whether the stimulus was visible through the left or the right eye.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the dominant eye effect.

claim: A closer look at the random slopes of the previous answer effect reveals three different strategies: some subjects tend to stick the same answer, some are balanced without any trend, and some tend to regularly alternate their answers.
source: Indeed, a closer look at the random slopes of the effect reveals three different strategies: Some subjects tend to stick the same answer, some subjects are balanced in their answers without any trend, and some subjects tend to regularly alternate their answers in each trial.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the random effects data.

claim: The previous answer behavior does not seem to influence any of the other effects, with no correlation between the random effects except for the correlation between the n-1 effect and the intercept (−0.55).
source: Note that this behavior does not seem to influence any of the other effects: We do not see any correlation between the random effects, except for the correlation between the n-1 effect and the intercept (−0.55, CI: −0.72,–0.34).
evidence: This is a data-based finding from the combined model.

claim: The correlation between the n-1 effect and the intercept means that subjects who tend to alternate their key presses will not have a strong bias in the intercept, or subjects who press the same key all the time also have a bias towards this key.
source: This correlation means that subjects who tend to alternate their key presses will not have a strong bias in the intercept, or the other way around, subjects who press the same key all the time also have a bias towards this key.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the correlation finding.

claim: Extended models showed no effect when both stimuli were in the temporal field, nor any three-way interaction.
source: Other extended models we considered showed no effect when both stimuli were in the temporal field, nor any three-way interaction.
evidence: This is a data-based finding from extended model testing.

claim: Variables showing no effect were removed from the final model following standard procedures to avoid spurious effects of unnecessary degrees of freedom.
source: Following standard procedures to avoid spurious effects of unnecessary degrees of freedom, we removed these variables from the final model.
evidence: This is a methodological detail about model selection.
